newsitem.title: USA: Caen wrote America's longest-running column.
newsitem.headline: Caen wrote America's longest-running column.

text.p: Legendary newspaper columnist Herb Caen, who died of cancer on Saturday, entertained readers for nearly 60 years with his witty and sometimes poignant reflections on life in San Francisco.
The Pulitzer prize-winning journalist, who wrote America's longest-running daily newspaper column, died at Pacific Medical Centre in San Francisco, the San Francisco Chronicle said.
Dubbed "Mr San Francisco", he became as synonymous with the city as the Golden Gate Bridge and had a large, devoted readership.
The Sacramento-born Caen, who moved to San Francisco at the age of 20 to take a newspaper job, had a life-long love affair with the city which he called "Baghdad-by-the-Bay".
For decades, he hammered out six daily columns a week on his trusty Royal typewriter, only in recent years cutting back to five columns a week in the San Francisco Chronicle.

Caen, usually impeccably dressed in a suit and fedora, had an eventful year in 1996. A week after he turned 80, the Pulitzer Board awarded him a special prize for his "extraordinary and continuing contribution as a voice and conscience of his city." He also married for the fourth time, to long-time companion Ann Moller.

But in May, he told his readers he had inoperable lung cancer. "I do wish I could have told you that my long silences were indeed due to The World's Greatest Hangover," he wrote, with a flash of his old humour in an otherwise sad column.
Amid a huge outpouring of public support, San Francisco threw a huge party for Caen two weeks later, when a new bayside promenade named "Herb Caen Way..." was dedicated.
San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown, an old friend, and actors Robin Williams and Don Johnson were among the 75,000 people who turned out to honour Caen.
Despite undergoing cancer treatment, Caen kept writing the column, although less frequently.

A typical Caen column consisted of many small items, including gossip, jokes, funny stories, puns on names and the occasional scoop -- all joined together by Caen's trademark three dots and always packed with people's names.

"I like short items and punchy items and a couple of scoops in there and, I hope, a funny anecdote, a one-liner that somebody can take to lunch that day and wow the people with. People are in a hurry at breakfast time. Who wants to read essays?" he said last year at a party in the Chronicle newsroom celebrating his Pulitzer prize.
From time to time, Caen wrote a column in which he paid homage to San Francisco, its larger-than-life characters and its energy, a vitality he felt had dimmed somewhat since his youth.

Caen could not say which of his columns he liked best. "There are too many of them, thousands of columns. I got sort of carried away by the Vietnam War and I wrote some steam- heated columns about that," said Caen, who opposed the war.

"I wrote some columns against capital punishment I was rather happy with. But mostly I'm proud of the dailiness, day after day I can turn it out and it's not too bad and if there's a good joke in there I'm happy," he said.

Herbert Eugene Caen was born in Sacramento on April 3, 1916, the son of a billiards hall proprietor. At Sacramento High School, under the name "Raisin Caen", he wrote a column for the school newspaper entitled "Corridor Gossip."
He became a police reporter for The Sacramento Union newspaper in 1932 and was hired by The San Francisco Chronicle in 1936 to write a column about radio.

Two years later, the newspaper dropped the radio column but Caen talked the editors into letting him try a local interest column which made its debut on July 5, 1938. Caen hopped from club to club every night, hobnobbing with the city's movers and shakers and gathering material for his column.

Caen's early gossip columns were modelled after those of the legendary New York columnist Walter Winchell. Caen wrote that when he first met Winchell, Winchell put his arm around him and said: "This kid imitates me better than any other kid in the business."
In 1942, Caen joined the Air Force and was assigned to communications, reaching the rank of captain.
Back in San Francisco after the war, he published "The San Francisco Book" in 1948 and the successful "Baghdad-by-the-Bay" the following year.
In 1950, Caen left the Chronicle to join the rival San Francisco Examiner, but returned to the Chronicle in 1958 with a salary of $38,000, writing for the paper until now.
Caen's first three marriages -- to Beatrice Mathews, Sally Gilbert and Maria Theresa Shaw -- ended in divorce.
He is survived by his fourth wife Ann and by his son Christopher.
